*Published on September 10, 2026 at 5:15 PM by Pedro Nakashima*

![](cover.jpg)

This **introduction to pandas** opens with a warning that almost no tutorial gives you: a good share of the pandas material currently online teaches something that has stopped working. pandas 3.0 was released on [January 21, 2026](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/v3.0.0.html), and it changed two behaviors that appear in practically every course recorded before that date. One of them is subtle enough that you write the code, see no error at all, and still end up with data that was never modified. The sections below cover what pandas is, the two objects the whole library rests on, how to load and inspect a table, how to filter, group, and handle missing values — and, at the end, exactly what changed and why it matters for anyone learning today.

If you have not written any Python yet, the natural starting point is [why learning Python still pays off in 2026](/posts/learn-python-2026/index.qmd), because from here on I will assume you already know what a variable, a function, and a loop are.

## What pandas is

pandas is the library that gives Python the ability to work with **tables**: rows, columns, headers, types per column. It does what a spreadsheet does, with two differences that decide everything: the work is written as code, which makes it reproducible and auditable by someone else; and the size limit stops being your screen and becomes the memory of your machine.

In practice, pandas is where nearly every data analysis in Python begins. You read a CSV, an Excel file, a SQL query, or some JSON, turn it into a table, clean up whatever is dirty, group it, summarize it — and only then pass the result along to a chart, a statistical model, or a report.

## Series and DataFrame: the two objects that matter

The entire library is organized around two types, and understanding how they relate saves a great deal of confusion later.

A **Series** is a column: a sequence of values of the same type, with an index labeling each position. A **DataFrame** is the whole table: a set of Series sharing the same index. Select one column from a DataFrame and you get a Series; select several and you get another DataFrame.

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "product": ["coffee", "sugar", "coffee", "milk"],
    "state": ["MS", "MS", "SP", "SP"],
    "amount": [12.50, 8.90, 14.00, 6.75],
})

type(df)            # DataFrame
type(df["amount"])  # Series
```

The index is not decoration. It is what aligns your data when you combine two structures: adding two Series makes pandas match values by index label, not by position. That is one of the largest differences from a spreadsheet, and it is behind half of the surprising results beginners run into.

## Load your data and look at it before anything else

In real life the table comes from a file, and the most used function in the library is `read_csv`.

```python
df = pd.read_csv("sales.csv")
```

Before computing anything, look at what came in. Three commands, and skipping this step is the single most common origin of a wrong analysis:

```python
df.head()      # the first rows
df.info()      # columns, types, and how many non-null values
df.describe()  # count, mean, std, min, quartiles, max
```

`info()` is the most important of the three, because it answers two questions at once: did every column arrive with the type it should have, and where are values missing. A column of monetary amounts that arrives as text — because the file used a comma as the decimal separator, or carried a currency symbol — will concatenate strings instead of adding numbers, and `info()` exposes that immediately.

## Selecting and filtering

Selecting a column is straightforward, with square brackets. Filtering rows uses a boolean mask: you write a condition, pandas hands back a column of true and false, and only the true rows survive.

```python
df["amount"]                # one column (Series)
df[["product", "amount"]]   # two columns (DataFrame)
df[df["amount"] > 10]       # only rows above 10
```

To combine conditions, use `&` for "and", `|` for "or", and **always wrap each condition in parentheses** — Python's operator precedence would otherwise evaluate the expression in the wrong order.

```python
df[(df["state"] == "MS") & (df["amount"] > 10)]
```

When you want to filter rows **and** pick columns at the same time, the tool is `.loc`, which takes both at once:

```python
df.loc[df["state"] == "MS", "amount"]
```

## The error that raises no error

Here is the trap behind the warning at the top. Suppose you want to zero out the amounts for the MS rows. Writing it like this feels natural:

```python
df[df["state"] == "MS"]["amount"] = 0
```

This is called **chained assignment**: two indexing steps in a row, one `[...]` followed by another. In pandas 3.0, that code changes nothing at all. `df[df["state"] == "MS"]` produces a brand new object, the assignment lands on that new object, and it is discarded on the next line — the original `df` stays exactly as it was. The library emits a `ChainedAssignmentError`, but **it is a warning, not an exception**: the program keeps running, and if you are not reading your output, you will analyze data you believed you had fixed.

The correct form does everything in a single step, with `.loc`:

```python
df.loc[df["state"] == "MS", "amount"] = 0
```

It is worth explaining why this is an improvement rather than a nuisance. Before pandas 3.0, chained assignment was worse: sometimes it worked and sometimes it did not, depending on internal details of how the table happened to be laid out in memory. What existed then was the notorious `SettingWithCopyWarning`, a warning that fired even on correct code and that the community learned to silence with defensive `.copy()` calls. With [Copy-on-Write](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/copy_on_write.html) on by default, the behavior became one single thing in every case: it never works. A consistently wrong behavior is far better than an unpredictable one, because it can be learned once and for all.

## Grouping and summarizing

`groupby` is what turns a table of transactions into an answer. The logic has three beats: split the rows by a key, apply a calculation within each group, combine the results.

```python
df.groupby("product")["amount"].sum()
```

For more than one measure in the same step, use `agg`:

```python
df.groupby("state")["amount"].agg(["sum", "mean", "count"])
```

The result comes back with the grouping key as the index rather than an ordinary column, which matters when you save to a file or join with another table. If you would rather have the key as a column, `reset_index()` handles it.

## Missing values

Real data has holes, and pandas represents them as `NaN`. The general rule is that aggregation functions **ignore** missing values instead of propagating them: the sum of `[1.0, NaN, 3.0]` is `4.0`, the mean is `2.0`, and `count()` returns `2`, not `3`.

That is convenient and dangerous in equal measure. Convenient because a single empty cell does not turn your whole calculation into `NaN`; dangerous because a mean computed over half your observations does not announce that it was computed over half your observations. So the habit worth building is counting the missing values before aggregating:

```python
df.isna().sum()   # missing values per column
```

Only after knowing how many there are, and why they are missing, should you choose between dropping (`dropna`) and filling (`fillna`). Filling a missing value with the column mean is an analytical decision with consequences, not a technical cleanup step — and in a report, an expert opinion, or a paper, it is a decision that has to be written down.

## What changed in pandas 3.0

Two changes in version 3.0 directly affect anyone learning right now, because they contradict what older material shows on screen.

The first is Copy-on-Write, covered above: chained assignment stopped working for good, `SettingWithCopyWarning` was removed, and the defensive `.copy()` calls that existed only to silence it are no longer needed.

The second is the type of text columns. Through version 2, a column of strings showed up in `info()` as `object`, a generic type for anything that was not a number. Starting with 3.0 there is a dedicated type, and the same column shows up as `str`. If a tutorial shows `object` where your screen shows `str`, there is nothing wrong with your code — the tutorial predates January 2026.

The practical lesson reaches beyond pandas: when following any technical material, check which version it describes and which one you are running. `pd.__version__` answers the second question in one line.

## FAQ

### Do I need to know Python before learning pandas?

Yes, the basics. Variables, types, functions, loops, and list indexing are enough to start. You do not need object-oriented programming or advanced data structures.

### What is the difference between pandas and Excel?

Excel is excellent for inspecting data and for one-off tasks. pandas wins on three fronts: the work is recorded as code and can be repeated and checked by someone else; the volume of data is no longer capped by the spreadsheet; and the same analysis can be applied to a new file without redoing anything by hand.

### Should I use `[]` or `.loc` for filtering?

For reading rows, both work. For **modifying** values, always use `.loc`, in a single step. That is the rule that keeps chained assignment out of your code.

### Does pandas work for large datasets?

Up to the limit of your machine's memory, yes, and that covers the vast majority of cases. Above that there are alternatives with a similar API, such as Polars and Dask, but pandas remains the right starting point — the concepts of table, index, filter, and grouping are the same everywhere.

### Why is my code not changing the DataFrame?

Almost always chained assignment. Look for two indexing steps in a row (`df[...][...] = ...`) and rewrite it with `.loc` in a single step.

## Conclusion

- pandas organizes data into **Series** (a column) and **DataFrame** (a table), and the index is what aligns values across structures.
- Inspect before you compute: `head()`, `info()`, and `describe()` reveal a wrong type or a missing value before either becomes a wrong result.
- Filter with a boolean mask, parentheses around each condition, and use `.loc` when you need rows and columns at once.
- To **modify** values, use `.loc` in a single step: in pandas 3.0 chained assignment never works, and it fails silently, with a warning but no exception.
- Aggregations ignore `NaN` by default — count the missing values with `isna().sum()` before trusting a mean.
- Check the library version before following any tutorial: since January 2026, text columns are `str`, no longer `object`.
